name: Phendimetrazine
lead: Phendimetrazine (brand names include Bontril) is a prescription stimulant of the morpholine class used as an appetite suppressant. By reducing hunger while someone follows a calorie-restricted plan, it is used to help lower body weight and body fat, which changes how the face and body look. The US label indicates it as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted regimen in patients with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet or exercise alone. [1][2]

It acts largely as a prodrug: Wikipedia states roughly 30% of an oral dose is converted to phenmetrazine, a norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent. [2] It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US. [2] Phenmetrazine itself was introduced in Europe in the 1950s as the trade product Preludin, and phendimetrazine was developed from the same Boehringer Ingelheim chemistry. [2][11]

Published clinical evidence for obesity is older and sparse; reviews list phendimetrazine alongside phentermine, diethylpropion and benzphetamine as sympathomimetic drugs approved only for short-term use. [3][12] In bodybuilding and physique-focused forums it appears as one of several prescription options people ask about when cutting body fat. [13]

chain: Makes a calorie deficit easier to hold
Lower body fat and a leaner face and physique
angle.text: Phendimetrazine is prescribed to reduce appetite during a calorie-restricted diet. Lower body fat changes facial definition and overall physique, which is the route by which people in physique communities discuss it. The label frames it as a short course for people with obesity rather than a cosmetic drug.

infobox: Bontril, Bontril PDM, Adipost, Statobex and others [2]

paras: The appearance rationale is indirect: a stimulant that blunts appetite makes it easier for some people to stay in a calorie deficit, and sustained fat loss changes facial fullness and body composition. In physique communities, people preparing for a cut sometimes ask about prescribed appetite suppressants such as Bontril as an alternative to other tools. [13] Prescribing information does not describe any cosmetic indication, and Grokipedia notes the drug is not intended for cosmetic purposes. [4]

The label describes use for exogenous obesity as a short-term adjunct in patients with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet and exercise. [1] Grokipedia adds that use beyond about 12 weeks is not established and that tolerance limits long-term effect; it also reports average additional weight loss of 3 to 5 kg over 12 weeks in controlled trials of sympathomimetic agents, a figure not verified against primary trial reports. [4]

Drug-class reviews describe the older sympathomimetic anorectics as agents approved for periods of 12 weeks or less, in contrast with newer medicines approved for longer-term use. [12][14] A 2016 primary-care review groups phendimetrazine among stimulant options and notes that, because of misuse potential, many obesity medications are controlled substances. [15]

The label lists palpitations, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure and ischemic events, and central nervous system effects including overstimulation, restlessness, insomnia, agitation, tremor, headache and psychotic state. [1] It warns against combination with other anorectics, including over-the-counter and herbal products, and cites a case-control study linking anorectic use longer than three months to a 23-fold increase in pulmonary hypertension risk. [1] Valvular heart disease has been reported with some other anorectics, but the label says no case had been reported with phendimetrazine alone. [1] Safe use in pregnancy has not been established (Pregnancy Category C). [1]
A 2005 safety review of obesity drugs recounts the history of withdrawn anorectics and then reviews the safety of the agents then available, including phendimetrazine. [16]

Phendimetrazine is described as largely inactive itself, with activity coming from conversion to phenmetrazine; Wikipedia says this produces steadier exposure and that the compound is regarded as having lower abuse potential than phenmetrazine. [2] Adding an N-methyl group to phenmetrazine yields phendimetrazine, which Wikipedia describes as an amphetamine congener acting as a norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent after conversion. [2] A 2002 laboratory study examined its interaction and that of its metabolites with monoamine transporters in rat brain. [5]

Wikipedia gives an elimination half-life of about 19 to 24 hours, with hepatic metabolism and urinary excretion, while Grokipedia reports a shorter figure of about 3.7 hours for the parent drug; the sources differ. [2][4] Sustained-action formulations were studied as early as the 1960s and 1970s, including a 1968 controlled trial of sustained-action phendimetrazine in obesity and a 1975 study of availability from sustained and non-sustained formulations. [17][18]

Phendimetrazine is 3,4-dimethyl-2-phenylmorpholine (also called mephenmetrazine) and belongs to the phenylmorpholine class, structurally related to amphetamines. [2] It is supplied as the tartrate salt. [4]

Phenmetrazine was first patented by Boehringer Ingelheim in 1952 and entered clinical use in Europe in 1954 as an appetite suppressant; Wikipedia reports that its misuse led to withdrawal from many markets, and that phendimetrazine, its prodrug, largely replaced it. [11] A US patent covering the synthesis route of phendimetrazine, naming Werner Heel and Karl Zeile and assigned to C. H. Boehringer Sohn, dates to 1961. [2] Prescription anti-obesity drug use in the US was later tracked by national databases from 1991 to 2011, a period in which phentermine dominated and other short-term agents were prescribed less often. [7]

Phendimetrazine is Schedule III in the US, Schedule IV in Canada, Class B2 in Brazil, and is listed under Schedule III of the international Convention on Psychotropic Substances. [2] Germany restricts it to authorised trade and does not allow prescription. [2] A 2018 analysis examined US health-policy and insurance coverage of FDA-approved obesity drugs, and a 2013 study examined prescribing of anti-obesity drugs in the US. [6][7] A survey of physician obesity specialists found that nearly all prescribed medications and that phentermine was the one all recommended. [19]
Phendimetrazine appears by name in banned-stimulant lists that T Nation forum members have posted when discussing supplements and drug testing for athletes. [20][21]

Older controlled trials examined sustained-action phendimetrazine in obesity and its effect on plasma lipids in the 1960s and 1970s. [17][22] Reviews of obesity pharmacotherapy summarise this older evidence on noradrenergic anorectics, including phendimetrazine. [3][10][12] No studies found of phendimetrazine for appearance-related or cosmetic goals.

More recent human trials have studied phendimetrazine for a different purpose. A controlled study in nine cocaine-dependent volunteers evaluated its abuse potential, and a randomized trial examined how phendimetrazine maintenance influenced the effects of intranasal cocaine. [23][24] Registered US trials of these designs enrolled 11 and 30 participants. [8][9] These are not studies of weight loss. In animals, phendimetrazine reduced choice of cocaine over food in rhesus monkeys over 14 days of treatment, and rats showed cocaine-like discriminative effects. [25][26]

timeline.event: Boehringer Ingelheim patents phenmetrazine, the active metabolite of phendimetrazine. [11]
Phenmetrazine enters clinical use in Europe. [11]
A US patent assigned to Boehringer Ingelheim covers the synthesis route for phendimetrazine. [2]
A controlled trial of sustained-action phendimetrazine in obesity is published. [17]
A US trial of phendimetrazine and cocaine begins. [9]

lore.intro: Phendimetrazine is mentioned occasionally on bodybuilding forums as a prescribed appetite suppressant for cutting, and appears in banned-substance lists posted for athletes. [13][20]

claims.claim: A prescribed appetite suppressant like Bontril helps people cut body fat.
claims.believers: A forum poster preparing to cut asked whether a prescribed Bontril or a research compound would be the better option, noting that Bontril is known for controlling appetite. [13]
claims.experts: The label indicates phendimetrazine only as a short-term adjunct to caloric restriction for people with BMI of 30 or higher. [1] Reviews describe it as an older short-term agent. [12]

claims.claim: Phendimetrazine is detectable in or banned by sports testing.
claims.believers: Members of a T Nation thread list phendimetrazine among stimulants prohibited for athletes. [20][21]
claims.experts: The compound is a controlled stimulant in many jurisdictions. [2]

card.summary: Older prescription stimulant appetite suppressant, a phenmetrazine prodrug, labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment; controlled and not a cosmetic drug.
card.note: Schedule III controlled substance; label cites pulmonary hypertension association with long-term anorectic use.

quick.overview:
Phendimetrazine is a prescription stimulant that suppresses appetite. In the US it is labelled for short-term use with a reduced-calorie diet in people with obesity.

It is an older drug with limited modern trial data and is a controlled substance.
quick.mechanism: It is partly converted in the body to phenmetrazine, which releases norepinephrine and dopamine and reduces appetite.
quick.risks: The label lists raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, agitation and other stimulant effects, and cites a link between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension. Safe use in pregnancy is not established. Schedule III in the US.
